actions.justification: MANDATORY action with 10-minute deadline. Patient has critical vitals: HR 105, BP 100/65, RR 28, SpO2 85%. Must be formally assessed immediately per GOLD COPD guidelines.
MANDATORY action. Patient has severe respiratory compromise (SpO2 85%, RR 28) requiring immediate respiratory assessment to guide management per GOLD COPD guidelines.

MANDATORY action per GOLD COPD guidelines. ABG is critical to assess ventilatory failure, hypercapnia (CO2 retention common in GOLD Stage 4), and acid-base status which will guide oxygen therapy and NIV eligibility.

MANDATORY per guidelines and phase requirements. Chest X-ray is required to assess severity, identify pneumothorax, pneumonia, or other causes of exacerbation. Must be completed within 60-minute deadline.
GOLD guideline mandates bronchodilator within 30 minutes for severe COPD exacerbation. Patient has SpO2 85%, RR 28, HR 105 indicating severe exacerbation requiring immediate bronchodilation.

GOLD guidelines mandate NIV eligibility assessment for severe COPD exacerbation. Patient has severe hypoxemia (SpO2 85%), elevated RR (28), and likely hypercapnia (COPD Gold Stage 4 with cor pulmonale). NIV is the preferred respiratory support to avoid intubation and to avoid high-flow O2 risks in CO2 retainers.
Mandatory per GOLD COPD guidelines for severe exacerbation. Systemic corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation, shorten recovery time, and reduce treatment failure in COPD exacerbations.

Mandatory per GOLD COPD guidelines for severe exacerbation. Antibiotics are indicated given worsening dyspnea and signs of potential infectious trigger. Blood culture should ideally precede antibiotics if possible.

Patient has life-threatening hypoxemia (SpO2 85%). Supplemental oxygen should be administered with controlled titration to target SpO2 88-92% to correct hypoxemia while avoiding worsening hypercapnia via the Haldane effect in this COPD/cor pulmonale patient.

Patient has severe hypoxia (SpO2 85%) and hypotension (BP 100/65). Mental status assessment is critical to determine encephalopathy from hypercapnia/hypoxia, which would affect NIV tolerance and urgency of intubation decisions.

BMP is needed to assess renal function, electrolytes, and bicarbonate (chronic CO2 retention compensation). Also important given hypotension and signs of cor pulmonale — guides diuretic use and overall fluid/electrolyte management.

CBC will assess for polycythemia (common in GOLD stage 4 COPD with chronic hypoxia), leukocytosis suggesting bacterial infection driving the exacerbation, and anemia which could worsen oxygen delivery given the low SpO2.

Patient has GOLD stage 4 COPD with cor pulmonale and pulmonary hypertension presenting with severe exacerbation and SpO2 85%. Pulmonology expertise is critical for managing complex NIV decisions, ventilatory strategy, and cor pulmonale management.

Patient has MAP 77 with HR 105 and BP 100/65 — borderline hemodynamic compromise. Lactate helps assess tissue perfusion and rule out co-existing sepsis or hemodynamic failure contributing to presentation.

Procalcitonin helps guide antibiotic therapy duration and differentiate bacterial from viral etiology in COPD exacerbations per GOLD guidelines, supporting antibiotic stewardship in this complex patient.

Sputum culture is indicated in severe COPD exacerbation to identify causative pathogens and guide antibiotic therapy. This patient has signs of infection and already received empiric antibiotics; culture will help de-escalate or adjust therapy.

CT chest is warranted given the complex presentation with cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension, and severe hypoxia (SpO2 85%). It can identify pulmonary embolism (a common COPD exacerbation trigger), pneumothorax, or other structural causes of decompensation not visible on plain X-ray.

Blood cultures should be obtained in this severely ill patient with COPD exacerbation and signs of systemic stress (tachycardia, hypotension, low MAP) to rule out bacteremia before further antibiotic adjustments.

Patient has signs of right heart failure/cor pulmonale with bilateral leg edema, JVP elevation, and hepatomegaly. Diuretic therapy is indicated to reduce volume overload and decrease right ventricular preload, which may improve dyspnea and oxygenation in the context of cor pulmonale and pulmonary hypertension.

Patient has hypotension (BP 100/65, MAP 77) with signs of right heart failure (cor pulmonale, JVP elevation, hepatomegaly). Cautious IV fluid administration may support preload in the context of low MAP, though must be done carefully given pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. This is the only available action not yet completed.

Patient has MAP of 77 with HR 105 and SpO2 of 85%, suggesting hemodynamic compromise. If fluid challenge does not improve MAP adequately, vasopressor support (e.g., norepinephrine) may be needed to maintain perfusion pressure in the setting of cor pulmonale and severe COPD exacerbation.

Patient has cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension, tachycardia (HR 105), and hypotension — continuous ECG monitoring is indicated to detect arrhythmias or right heart strain patterns (S1Q3T3, RBBB) that can occur with severe COPD exacerbation and pulmonary hypertension.

Patient has SpO2 of 85% with supplemental oxygen already initiated; continuous pulse oximetry is essential to track response to therapy and detect deterioration in this severe COPD exacerbation with cor pulmonale.

Patient has bilateral leg edema, JVP elevation, and hepatomegaly consistent with cor pulmonale and right heart failure; diuretic has been given and fluid balance monitoring is critical to assess response and guide further management.
